props.title: Check the World, Not the Report

card.copy:
Check the World,
Not the Report

beats.narration_text: The agent completes its run and returns a status report. File deleted — check mark. Invoice paid — check mark. Support ticket closed — check mark. The report is complete, neatly formatted, confident in tone. Your job as an auditor is not to read that report and nod. Your job is to go look at the file, the bank account, the ticket system — the actual state of the world — and check whether the report describes it. Because a system can produce a perfect report about a thing it did not do. The report is not the world. It is the system's story about the world.

beats.narration_text: An audit that reads the system's output to verify the system's output has graded the shadow, not the wall. The shadow can be perfect while the wall stands untouched. This is not an edge case — it is the default failure mode of agentic systems. An agent that encounters an error during execution may log success anyway, because the success message was the easier path through its instruction set. An agent that partially completed a task may report full completion because partial completion was not a recognized output state. An agent that reversed its action may report it as completed because the reversal happened silently. The output is the system's view of itself. It is not the ground truth.

beats.narration_text: The Casebook assignment makes this concrete. You pick a system — your Pebble — and you audit its agentic failures. Every case you document has an 'actual outcome' field. The most common mistake is to fill that field with the system's own report: 'the system reported the file was deleted.' That is not an actual outcome. That is the shadow. The actual outcome requires naming the world state: 'the file was still present in the directory at path X, verified by running ls -la.' One sentence. The artifact is the report. The world is the directory. You checked the relationship between them.

beats.narration_text: The mechanism is artifact-world separation: name the artifact the system produces, name the world state the artifact claims to describe, and verify the relationship by checking the world directly — not the artifact again.

beats.image_description: A split-panel scene viewed from above: left panel labeled ARTIFACT — a tidy crimson report page with checkmarks, titled 'Agent Output'. Right panel labeled WORLD — a file directory, a bank ledger, a ticket system, all in teal. A gold flashlight beam crosses from the left panel to the right, illuminating the actual state. The right panel's world state does not match the report's claims — a file icon is still present where the report says 'deleted'. The flashlight circle highlights the discrepancy

beats.narration_text: The split-panel animation. Left side: the agent's report, formatted, complete, timestamped, confident. Right side: the actual system state at the same timestamp. The agent's report says 'invoice paid.' The payment system shows the payment in PENDING status. The agent's report says 'file deleted.' The file system shows the file, intact, at its original path. The agent's report says 'ticket closed.' The ticketing system shows it OPEN, reassigned. The auditor's flashlight sweeps from left to right — not to admire the report, but to check each claim against the world state on the right side of the panel. Three claims. Three mismatches. The report is not wrong by intention. The system had no way to know what it did not know. The audit did.

beats.narration_text: Practically: the world-check requires external access. You cannot check the file system from inside the agent's output log. You need to go to the file system — open a terminal, run ls, read the directory state. You need to go to the payment system — open the ledger, read the transaction status. The world-check is always an out-of-band verification. If your audit requires only reading the agent's own outputs, you have not left the artifact. You are still reading the shadow. The distinction is not philosophical — it is operational. Which source of data are you reading to establish ground truth?

beats.narration_text: The Casebook implication is precise: every case your casebook documents must include a world-state check, not a report-read. 'The system reported success' is never an actual outcome. The actual outcome is what you found when you went and looked. For a file operation: what was the directory state. For a message send: what appeared in the inbox. For a database write: what the database returned when you queried it. The sentence that starts 'I verified by...' is the sentence that distinguishes an audited case from a repeated performance review.

beats.narration_text: The broader design implication: agentic systems that rely on their own output as ground truth have no way to detect their own silent failures. A complete agentic pipeline needs an independent verification step that checks world state after every high-blast-radius action — not by reading the agent's log, but by querying the system the action affected. Verification is a separate read from a separate source. The agent's success message is not verification. It is the thing being verified.

beats.narration_text: The epistemic implication is the deepest one: a system that cannot distinguish 'I did the thing' from 'I produced a report that says I did the thing' is not a reliable executor. It is a confident writer. Confidence in tone is not confidence in outcome. The auditor's role is to hold the distinction between the artifact and the world, and to check the relationship between them every single time. Not because the system is malicious — it is not. But because the system has no way to check its own ground truth. You do.

beats.narration_text: A student submits their Casebook with ten cases. Case 4 documents the system deleting a user account. Actual outcome field: 'The system reported: User account deleted successfully. Status: 200 OK.' The grader reads the case and writes: this is not an actual outcome. This is the artifact. Where is the world-check? The student returns to their notes. They open the admin panel and query the user account. It is still there, deactivated but not deleted — the system had mapped 'delete' to 'deactivate' because hard deletion required a separate admin flag the agent never set. The report was truthful from the system's perspective. The world state was different. The rewritten actual outcome reads: 'Queried the admin panel at path /admin/users/{id}. Account status was DEACTIVATED, not deleted. The hard-delete flag was not set. The system's 200 OK response described a successful deactivation, not the deletion the prompt requested.' That is a case. The first version was a report-read. The second is a world-check.

beats.narration_text: An audit that reads the system's output has graded the shadow. The world-check is a separate read from a separate source that verifies the actual state of the thing the system claimed to change. Name the artifact — the report. Name the world — the directory, the ledger, the inbox. Check the relationship by querying the world directly. In the Casebook: every actual outcome field must describe what you found when you went and looked — never what the system reported. The report is what you are checking. It is not how you check.
